title: Primary Function
learningObjectives: Connect parting function to lateral stiffness.
student: State the purpose of the parting tool and explain why the blade must remain laterally stiff while penetrating the workpiece.
instructor: The insert parts the rotating workpiece while the thin blade supports it. Lateral stiffness helps keep the blade body within the wider groove and limits side contact or run-off.

title: External Load and Constraint
student: The lead-angle configuration produces the given F_L at the cutting end. Identify its direction relative to blade length and the holder restraint. Explain why this component causes sideways weak-axis bending rather than representing the main tangential cutting force.
instructor: F_L is the axial/lateral component associated with the inclined edge. It acts transverse to the blade's longitudinal axis in plan view; the holder supplies the fixed restraint, causing weak-axis bending.

title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
student: Idealize the effectively unsupported blade segment as a cantilever and identify the fixed and free/cutting ends.
instructor: The holder/clamp is the equivalent fixed end; the cutting insert is at the free end of the effective unsupported segment.

title: Load Path
student: Trace the lateral load from the cutting insert through the thin blade body into the tool holder.
instructor: The lead-angle lateral component enters at the insert, transfers through the blade as shear and bending, and is reacted by the clamped holder.

title: Critical Component and Locations
student: Identify the critical component and locations for weak-axis bending stress and lateral deflection.
instructor: The blade body is critical. Fixed-end moment and stress are largest at the holder section, while lateral displacement is largest at the cutting tip.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
student: Identify the primary response and explain why comparing lateral tip deflection with one-side cut clearance is the main engineering decision. Identify bending stress as a secondary response.
instructor: The primary decision is whether delta_L remains below c. Weak-axis bending stress is also calculated, but it does not replace the clearance comparison.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify inputs controlling clearance and response.
student: Identify L, b, H, E, F_L, s, and c and state how each affects clearance, stiffness, deflection, or stress.
instructor: s and b establish clearance; H and b establish I_y; F_L, L, E, and I_y control deflection; F_L and L also determine moment.

title: Student-Generated Idealization
student: Draw a top/plan-view cantilever model showing the holder, L, F_L, b, H, s, c, and delta_L. Include an FBD.
instructor: A complete model shows the equivalent fixed holder, straight blade, cutting tip, transverse F_L, weak-axis rectangular section, cut walls, and lateral tip displacement.

title: Modeling Assumptions
student: State assumptions needed to reduce the real parting operation to the simplified beam and clearance model.
instructor: Use a linearly elastic rectangular blade, small deformation, concentrated static equivalent F_L, centered cut, equal nominal side clearance, rigid holder, and effective unsupported length. Neglect holder/insert compliance, varying force, chatter, thermal effects, wear, chips, and nonlinear wall contact.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
student: Outline the sequence for clearance, weak-axis I_y, deflection, acceptance, utilization/margin, moment/stress, L_max, and final interpretation.
instructor: Find c, compute I_y, calculate delta_L, compare delta_L with c, quantify utilization and margin, calculate moment/stress, solve delta_L=c for L_max, compare with T_max, and state limitations.

title: Available Side Clearance
student: Calculate c=(s-b)/2 and explain the centered-cut assumption.

title: Weak-Axis Section Property
student: Calculate I_y=Hb^3/12 and explain why the thin dimension strongly affects lateral stiffness.
instructor: I_y = {{parting_Iy_mm4}} mm4. The weak-axis thickness is cubed.

title: Clearance Assessment
student: Compare delta_L with c. State the relation and simplified acceptance result, then calculate clearance utilization and remaining margin.
instructor: delta_L {{parting_clearance_relation}} c. {{parting_acceptance}} Utilization is {{parting_utilization_pct}}%; remaining margin is {{parting_margin_mm}} mm.

title: Fixed-End Bending Response
student: Calculate M_max=F_L L and sigma_max=M_max(b/2)/I_y. Keep the deflection-clearance comparison as the primary decision.

title: Maximum Effective Overhang
student: Set delta_L=c and calculate L_max=[3EI_yc/F_L]^(1/3). Interpret this as an effective overhang in the simplified model.

title: Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: Compare clearance and published depth with limitations.
student: State the clearance result, compare L_max with T_max, and explain why this static check does not establish chatter-free operation, full machining stability, or a manufacturer-approved limit.
